subtopic_detail: Toddler refusing to use an arm after axial traction, held pronated, with no focal bone tenderness and pain only on forearm rotation
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 2 year old girl who has not used her left arm since her older brother swung her up by both hands at the playground an hour ago. Her mother says she cried for a minute, then settled, and has since been eating and playing one handed.

There was no fall and nothing struck the arm. She lets you touch the whole limb without complaint, and only cries when the forearm is turned.

data_table.Examination: Left arm held slightly flexed and pronated against the trunk, no swelling, bruising or deformity, no focal tenderness over the clavicle, humerus, olecranon, radius or ulna, full passive shoulder movement, resists supination of the forearm, hand warm with radial pulse present and capillary refill under 2 seconds

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Apply a broad arm sling and review her in fracture clinic in seven days
options.rationale: Slinging treats a presumed fracture and leaves a reducible subluxation in place for a week, during which the child continues not to use the arm. Slings are also poorly tolerated at this age and are not part of the management of a subluxed radial head. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

options.text: Perform a supination and flexion manoeuvre at the elbow without imaging
options.rationale: Axial traction on an extended pronated arm displaces the annular ligament over the radial head, and the diagnosis is made on the mechanism plus the absence of swelling, deformity and focal bone tenderness. Reduction by supination then flexion, or by hyperpronation, is done at the bedside and most children use the arm again within 30 minutes. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

options.text: Request radiographs of the left elbow before attempting any manipulation
options.rationale: Radiographs are reserved for an atypical mechanism, swelling, deformity, focal bone tenderness, or failure of two reduction attempts, none of which apply here. Films in this setting are usually normal and delay a manoeuvre that is both diagnostic and therapeutic. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

options.text: Request radiographs of the left clavicle, humerus and forearm today
options.rationale: A pseudoparalysed arm in a toddler does raise clavicular and humeral injury, but each of those requires a fall or a direct blow and produces localised tenderness over the injured bone. Both are absent, which is what separates this presentation from an occult fracture. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

options.text: Immobilise in an above elbow backslab and review clinically in ten days
options.rationale: Backslabbing is the answer for a suspected undisplaced fracture with normal initial films, such as a toddler fracture of the tibia after a twisting fall. Here the mechanism is longitudinal traction and there is no bone tenderness, so immobilisation treats the wrong problem. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

explanation.summary: Radial head subluxation is the commonest elbow injury of early childhood and peaks between one and four years, when the annular ligament is still lax enough to slip over the radial head under longitudinal traction. The child characteristically refuses to use the limb rather than localising pain, which can be misread as a fracture or even as a brachial plexus problem. The whole diagnosis rests on the mechanism plus a normal palpation of every long bone in the limb, and the treatment is a bedside manoeuvre. Radiographs are for the child whose story or examination does not fit, or whose arm does not recover after two attempts.
key_points: Mechanism is axial traction on a pronated extended arm, not a fall or a blow
The arm is held flexed and pronated with no swelling, deformity or bone tenderness
Supination with flexion, or hyperpronation, reduces it at the bedside
Imaging is indicated only for atypical features or failure of two attempts
Return of spontaneous use within 30 minutes confirms the diagnosis
explanation.pearls: If the child is still not using the arm 30 minutes after a second reduction attempt, abandon the diagnosis and radiograph the elbow, because a supracondylar or radial neck fracture presents identically in a toddler who cannot localise pain.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Radial head subluxation

subtopic_detail: Limping toddler with focal tibial tenderness after a low energy twisting fall and radiographs reported as normal
stem:
You are the emergency department resident seeing a 20 month old boy who caught his foot at the bottom of a slide yesterday and twisted as he came down. Since then he will crawl and will stand if held, but screams and lifts the right leg whenever he tries to take a step.

He is afebrile, has been well, and has had no recent illness. His mother has seen no swelling and the leg looks straight to her.

data_table.Examination: No effusion, warmth or restriction at the right hip, knee or ankle, full painless passive rotation of the hip, point tenderness over the mid to distal right tibial shaft, no bruising or deformity, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the right tibia and fibula reported as no fracture identified; C reactive protein 4 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Apply an above knee cast or boot and arrange clinical review in two weeks
options.rationale: An undisplaced spiral fracture of the tibia after a low energy twisting injury is frequently invisible on initial films, and focal tibial tenderness with a consistent mechanism is enough to treat it as one. Immobilisation gives comfort and protection, and the diagnosis is confirmed at review by periosteal reaction rather than by repeating films early. (Source: RCH CPG: Limp)

options.text: Arrange an urgent hip ultrasound and review the result the same afternoon
options.rationale: Hip ultrasound looks for the effusion of transient synovitis or septic arthritis, both of which restrict and pain passive hip rotation. Full painless hip rotation with tenderness localised to the tibial shaft points away from the hip entirely. (Source: RCH CPG: Limp)

options.text: Admit for intravenous flucloxacillin after taking blood cultures on arrival
options.rationale: Focal bone tenderness does raise osteomyelitis, which is why the history matters: this child is afebrile, well, and has a clear mechanical trigger the day before with a normal C reactive protein. Osteomyelitis in a toddler usually shows fever, systemic upset or raised inflammatory markers. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute osteomyelitis)

options.text: Discharge with simple analgesia and advice to mobilise as pain allows
options.rationale: Simple analgesia alone is reasonable for a soft tissue injury with diffuse tenderness, but not when tenderness is point localised over a long bone. Walking on an unprotected undisplaced fracture prolongs pain and risks displacement. (Source: RCH CPG: Limp)

options.text: Arrange a whole body bone scan through the radiology department this week
options.rationale: Bone scanning belongs to the limping child with no localising signs and no mechanism, where the site of pathology is genuinely unknown. Here the mechanism and the tender point already identify the bone, so the scan adds radiation without changing treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Limp)

explanation.summary: The toddler fracture is an undisplaced spiral fracture of the tibial shaft produced by a twisting force in a child who has recently begun walking, and it is the commonest cause of an acute atraumatic looking limp in this age group. Initial radiographs miss a substantial proportion because the fracture line is hairline and may be visible in only one plane. The decision to treat therefore rests on the mechanism and on point tenderness over the tibia, not on the film. The differential that must be actively excluded is infection, which is why fever, systemic upset and inflammatory markers are checked before committing to a mechanical diagnosis.
key_points: Low energy twisting injury in a newly walking child is the classic mechanism
Initial radiographs are commonly normal, so a negative film does not exclude it
Point tenderness over the tibial shaft with a normal hip examination localises it
Above knee immobilisation for two to three weeks is the usual treatment
Fever or raised inflammatory markers should redirect towards osteomyelitis
explanation.pearls: Periosteal new bone becomes visible on repeat radiographs about ten to fourteen days after a toddler fracture, so a film taken at the two week review confirms the diagnosis retrospectively while an immediate repeat film usually does not.

subtopic_detail: Newborn with inturned feet distinguishing a rigid deformity requiring serial casting from one that corrects passively to neutral
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar performing the newborn examination on a term baby girl on day one. The midwife has asked you to look at her feet, which both point inwards, and her parents want to know whether she will need an operation.

The pregnancy was uncomplicated with normal liquor volume and no breech presentation. She is feeding, moving all four limbs and has a normal neurological examination.

data_table.Examination: Both forefeet are adducted and the heels are turned inwards, the right hindfoot is fixed in equinus and cannot be brought past 20 degrees of plantarflexion, the left foot can be brought to a neutral ankle position and the lateral border straightened with gentle pressure, deep medial and posterior creases on the right only, right calf circumference 1 cm less than the left, hips stable with negative Ortolani and Barlow tests, spine intact with no dimple or hair tuft

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management for the right foot?

options.text: Reassure the parents and teach them passive stretching at each nappy change
options.rationale: Passive stretching is the treatment for a positional deformity, which is defined by being correctable to neutral by gentle hand pressure, as the left foot is here. A hindfoot that cannot be brought out of equinus will not respond to stretching and will stiffen further if casting is delayed. (Source: RCH CPG: Talipes)

options.text: Refer for serial casting with a view to starting in the first weeks of life
options.rationale: A rigid equinus hindfoot with medial and posterior creases and calf wasting is a structural deformity rather than an intrauterine packing problem, and the Ponseti method of weekly manipulation and above knee casting is the first line treatment in Australia. Starting within the first few weeks exploits ligamentous laxity and reduces the proportion of children who need extensive surgery. (Source: RCH CPG: Talipes)

options.text: Arrange hip ultrasound at six weeks and orthopaedic review of the feet after that
options.rationale: Hip imaging is appropriate where a risk factor for developmental dysplasia is present, but this baby was not breech, has a normal family history and has stable hips on examination. Waiting six weeks before addressing a rigid foot also wastes the period of greatest correctability. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

options.text: Refer for surgical soft tissue release to be performed at three months of age
options.rationale: Primary surgical release was the historical approach and is now reserved for deformity that resists or relapses after a full casting programme. Operating before casting produces a stiffer, more painful foot in the long term than the same result achieved by manipulation. (Source: RCH CPG: Talipes)

options.text: Apply below knee strapping on the ward and review her in clinic at six weeks
options.rationale: Strapping below the knee cannot hold the corrected position because the deformity includes hindfoot equinus, which requires the knee to be flexed and included in the cast. Below knee immobilisation allows the foot to rotate within the cast and correction is lost. (Source: RCH CPG: Talipes)

explanation.summary: Inturned feet at birth span a spectrum from a positional deformity caused by intrauterine crowding, which corrects passively and needs only reassurance, to a structural deformity with fixed hindfoot equinus, cavus and forefoot adduction. The examination that separates them is whether the foot can be brought to a neutral ankle with gentle pressure, supported by secondary signs of a true structural problem such as deep creases and a smaller calf. Structural deformity is treated by the Ponseti method, usually with a percutaneous tendo Achilles tenotomy at the end of the casting sequence, followed by a foot abduction brace for several years. Relapse is driven almost entirely by brace non adherence, so parental counselling at the outset matters as much as the casts.
key_points: Correctability to neutral by gentle pressure defines a positional deformity
Fixed equinus, deep creases and calf wasting indicate a structural deformity
Serial manipulation and above knee casting is first line and starts within weeks
Most children need a tendo Achilles tenotomy before the final cast
Long term bracing is required and non adherence is the main cause of relapse
explanation.pearls: The foot abduction brace after Ponseti casting is worn 23 hours a day for three months and then at night until about age four, and stopping it early is the single strongest predictor of recurrence.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

subtopic_detail: Napkin area rash involving the skin creases with separate small lesions beyond the main red area after a week of barrier cream
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 7 month old boy whose nappy rash has not settled despite a week of zinc barrier paste applied at every change. His mother says the redness now runs right into the skin folds at the tops of his legs, and that there are a few separate red spots on his tummy just above the nappy line.

He finished a course of oral amoxicillin for otitis media ten days ago. He is feeding normally, growing along the 50th centile and is otherwise well.

data_table.Examination: Confluent beefy red erythema over the perineum and buttocks extending into the inguinal and gluteal creases, a collarette of fine scale at the margin, several discrete red papules and small pustules on skin beyond the main plaque, no vesicles, no honey coloured crust, no ulceration, oral mucosa clear, no lymphadenopathy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Apply a topical imidazole antifungal to the affected area at each nappy change
options.rationale: Involvement of the skin creases with satellite papules and pustules beyond the confluent area is the pattern of candidal infection, which is favoured by the recent antibiotic course. A topical imidazole such as clotrimazole or miconazole applied with each change, continued for a week after clearance, is the treatment. (Source: RCH CPG: Napkin rash)

options.text: Continue the barrier paste and add frequent nappy free time each day
options.rationale: Barrier preparations and air exposure are the treatment for irritant dermatitis, which characteristically spares the creases because urine and faeces do not reach them. This rash involves the creases and has already failed a week of exactly this approach. (Source: RCH CPG: Napkin rash)

options.text: Apply a moderately potent topical corticosteroid ointment twice daily for a week
options.rationale: Moderate and high potency steroids are avoided under a nappy because occlusion greatly increases absorption and risks atrophy and striae in thin infant skin. Steroids also worsen untreated candidal infection by suppressing the local inflammatory response. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Prescribe oral cefalexin for seven days and review the rash at the end of it
options.rationale: Oral antibiotics treat bacterial superinfection, which presents with honey coloured crusting, pustules concentrated within the plaque, or systemic upset rather than a creased distribution with outlying lesions. A further antibiotic course would in fact make candidal overgrowth worse. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Take a skin scraping for fungal culture and withhold treatment until it returns
options.rationale: Microscopy and culture are reserved for rash that fails appropriate antifungal treatment or where an unusual organism is suspected. The clinical pattern here is diagnostic enough to treat, and waiting several days for a culture leaves a distressed infant untreated. (Source: RCH CPG: Napkin rash)

explanation.summary: Napkin rash is usually an irritant contact dermatitis from prolonged contact with urine and faeces, and its signature is that it affects the convex surfaces and spares the depths of the creases. Candidal infection is the common secondary problem, and it reverses that distribution by growing preferentially in the warm moist folds while throwing off satellite lesions onto adjacent skin. Recent antibiotics, recent diarrhoea and a rash that has failed barrier treatment all raise the likelihood. Rash that fails a proper antifungal course should prompt reconsideration of seborrhoeic dermatitis, psoriasis, zinc deficiency or, rarely, Langerhans cell histiocytosis.
key_points: Irritant napkin dermatitis spares the creases, candidal infection involves them
Satellite papules and pustules beyond the main plaque are the key sign
Recent antibiotic exposure is a common precipitant in infants
Topical imidazole at each change is first line, continued a week after clearing
Potent steroids are avoided under the occlusion of a nappy
explanation.pearls: A napkin rash that persists despite both barrier and antifungal treatment, especially with petechiae or erosions in the folds, should prompt consideration of Langerhans cell histiocytosis and dermatology referral rather than a further topical trial.

subtopic_detail: Preschool girl whose vulval skin appears fused in the midline with a normal urinary stream and no symptoms
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 3 year old girl whose mother noticed while bathing her that the skin between her legs looks joined together, and is worried that something is blocked or that she has been interfered with.

The child passes urine in a single steady stream, is dry by day, has no pain, no itch and no discharge, and has never had a urinary infection. She is thriving, her behaviour is unchanged and there are no child protection concerns raised by the history.

data_table.Examination: The labia minora are joined in the midline by a thin translucent membrane with a visible pale central line, an opening of about 4 mm remains anteriorly, no erythema, no excoriation, no bruising or tears, no discharge, perineum and anus otherwise normal
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative for leucocytes, nitrites and blood

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer to a paediatric surgeon for division of the membrane under anaesthesia
options.rationale: Surgical division is reserved for adhesions causing urinary obstruction, recurrent infection or symptoms that persist after topical treatment. It carries a high recurrence rate while the child remains oestrogen deficient, so it is not a first response to an asymptomatic finding. (Source: RCH CPG: Labial adhesions)

options.text: Separate the adhesion manually in the clinic room using lubricant and traction
options.rationale: Forcible separation is painful, frequently bleeds, and creates raw surfaces that readhere more firmly than before. It also risks a frightening genital examination for a child in whom nothing needs fixing. (Source: RCH CPG: Labial adhesions)

options.text: Explain the natural history, advise on hygiene, and review her as needed
options.rationale: Labial adhesion is an acquired consequence of the low oestrogen state of childhood and resolves spontaneously around puberty in the great majority, with many separating earlier. With a normal stream, no infections and no symptoms there is nothing to treat, so explanation plus avoidance of soaps and bubble baths is the management. (Source: RCH CPG: Labial adhesions)

options.text: Prescribe topical oestrogen cream to the midline nightly for six to eight weeks
options.rationale: Topical oestrogen is the treatment when adhesions obstruct the stream, cause pooling with post void dribbling or drive recurrent urinary infection, none of which apply here. It also causes breast budding and vulval pigmentation with prolonged use, so it is not used for cosmetic indications. (Source: RCH CPG: Labial adhesions)

options.text: Refer to the child protection unit for a formal forensic medical examination
options.rationale: Labial adhesion is not a finding associated with sexual abuse, and the examination shows no bruising, tears or other injury and no concerning history or behaviour change. Referral on this finding alone subjects the child to an unnecessary examination. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

explanation.summary: Labial adhesion affects up to around two percent of prepubertal girls and arises because the unoestrogenised vulval epithelium is thin and sticks together after minor irritation. It is usually an incidental finding on bathing or nappy changing and parents commonly fear either an obstruction or abuse, so the consultation is largely about explanation. Treatment is directed only at symptoms, with topical oestrogen for obstruction, pooling or recurrent infection, and surgery reserved for failure of that. The adhesion resolves as endogenous oestrogen rises at puberty, and recurrence after any treatment is common until then.
key_points: It is acquired from the low oestrogen state of childhood, not congenital
Asymptomatic adhesion with a normal stream needs explanation only
Topical oestrogen is reserved for obstruction, pooling or recurrent infection
Forcible separation causes bleeding and firmer readherence
It is not a sign of sexual abuse in the absence of other findings
explanation.pearls: Topical oestrogen applied to the fusion line for more than about six to eight weeks can produce breast budding and vulval pigmentation, both of which reverse on stopping, so courses are time limited and reviewed rather than repeated indefinitely.

subtopic_detail: Flat pink birthmark present from birth covering the forehead and upper eyelid on one side of a newborn
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar asked to review a term newborn boy on day two because of a birthmark that the midwife says has been there since delivery and has not changed.

His parents are distressed and have been told by a relative that it will fade like a stork mark. He is feeding, alert and moving all limbs symmetrically, and there have been no abnormal movements.

data_table.Examination: A flat pink patch with a sharp midline border covering the left forehead, upper eyelid and the skin in front of the ear, not raised and not blanching fully on pressure, red reflex present bilaterally, pupils equal and reactive, no corneal enlargement or cloudiness, anterior fontanelle soft, tone and primitive reflexes symmetrical

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the parents that this will fade over the first year and arrange no follow up
options.rationale: Fading is the natural history of the salmon patch, which sits on the glabella, eyelids or nape, is symmetrical and blanches readily. A unilateral capillary malformation respecting the midline persists, darkens and thickens with age. (Source: RCH CPG: Vascular malformations)

options.text: Start oral propranolol after a baseline heart rate and blood glucose measurement
options.rationale: Propranolol shrinks proliferating infantile haemangiomas, which are absent or faint at birth and then grow rapidly over weeks. A capillary malformation is fully formed at birth and static, and does not respond to beta blockade. (Source: RCH CPG: Haemangioma of infancy)

options.text: Refer him for pulsed dye laser treatment to the patch at around twelve months
options.rationale: Pulsed dye laser is the established treatment for the cutaneous mark and is often started in infancy, so this is part of the plan rather than wrong in itself. It does not address the ocular and intracranial risks, which are the time critical part of the assessment. (Source: RCH CPG: Vascular malformations)

options.text: Refer for ophthalmology review including measurement of intraocular pressure
options.rationale: A capillary malformation involving the forehead and upper eyelid carries a substantial risk of ipsilateral glaucoma, which is present at birth in about half of affected children and can otherwise appear at any age, and of leptomeningeal angiomatosis. Glaucoma in infancy is silent until the eye is damaged, so early and repeated intraocular pressure measurement is the priority, alongside neurology input and imaging. (Source: RCH CPG: Vascular malformations)

options.text: Arrange a skin biopsy of the edge of the lesion before any specialist referral
options.rationale: Biopsy is not required because capillary malformation is a clinical diagnosis based on a flat, sharply demarcated, persistent patch present from birth. It also delays the assessments that actually change outcome and leaves a scar on the face. (Source: RCH CPG: Vascular malformations)

explanation.summary: A capillary malformation is a permanent developmental anomaly of dermal capillaries, present and fully formed at birth, and is distinguished from the common salmon patch by its unilateral distribution, sharp midline border and failure to fade. When it involves the skin supplied by the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, particularly the forehead and upper eyelid, it is associated with Sturge Weber syndrome. The two associated problems are ipsilateral glaucoma, which is frequently congenital and silent, and a leptomeningeal vascular malformation that causes seizures, hemiparesis and developmental impairment. Management is therefore multidisciplinary, combining lifelong ophthalmic pressure surveillance, neurological assessment with magnetic resonance imaging, and pulsed dye laser for the skin.
key_points: Capillary malformation is present at birth, persists and darkens over decades
Salmon patch is symmetrical, blanches readily and fades in the first year
Forehead and upper eyelid involvement raises Sturge Weber syndrome
Ipsilateral glaucoma is common, often congenital, and initially asymptomatic
Leptomeningeal involvement causes seizures and warrants neurology review
explanation.pearls: Intraocular pressure in a child with a forehead capillary malformation needs checking at diagnosis and then periodically for life, because glaucoma develops after infancy in a substantial minority whose first examination was entirely normal.

subtopic_detail: School aged child with multiple flat brown skin patches and freckling in the armpits and groins referred for a suspected genetic condition
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 7 year old girl whose mother has counted more than six flat coffee coloured patches on her trunk and limbs, some present since she was a baby and others appearing since she started school. Her mother has noticed clusters of small freckles under both arms and in the groin creases.

She is performing at the level expected for her year, has had no seizures and no headaches. No family member has a similar skin appearance.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 98/60 mmHg, other vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Eight flat light brown macules ranging from 8 to 22 mm on the trunk and limbs, freckling in both axillae and both groins, two small soft skin coloured nodules on the trunk, height and head circumference on the 50th centile, visual acuity 6/6 both eyes, no scoliosis, no bowing of the long bones, neurological examination unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits within the next month
options.rationale: Routine neuroimaging of an asymptomatic child is not recommended, because incidental findings are common and the optic pathway tumours it might detect are managed on the basis of visual and clinical progression rather than on images alone. Imaging is triggered by declining acuity, proptosis, precocious puberty or new neurological signs. (Source: RCH CPG: Neurofibromatosis type 1)

options.text: Refer to a paediatric dermatologist for laser treatment of the pigmented patches
options.rationale: The flat brown macules are asymptomatic markers of the underlying condition and are not treated, unlike the dermal neurofibromas that may be removed later for symptoms or appearance. Directing care at the pigmentation misses the systemic surveillance that determines outcome. (Source: RCH CPG: Neurofibromatosis type 1)

options.text: Reassure the family that pigmented patches are common and require no follow up
options.rationale: One or two flat brown macules are indeed a common and benign finding in healthy children and need nothing. Six or more of them combined with skin fold freckling meets established diagnostic criteria, which changes the finding from incidental to diagnostic. (Source: RCH CPG: Neurofibromatosis type 1)

options.text: Send genetic testing and defer any further assessment until the result returns
options.rationale: Molecular testing is useful where the clinical picture is incomplete, in a young child with pigmentation alone, or for reproductive counselling. Where criteria are already met clinically the diagnosis does not wait on a result, and deferring surveillance is what causes harm. (Source: RCH CPG: Neurofibromatosis type 1)

options.text: Begin annual review including blood pressure, vision, spine and development
options.rationale: Six or more flat brown macules over 5 mm with axillary or inguinal freckling satisfies the clinical diagnostic criteria for neurofibromatosis type 1, so the task is surveillance rather than further confirmation. Annual review targets the complications that are treatable if found early, principally hypertension from renal artery stenosis or phaeochromocytoma, optic pathway glioma, scoliosis and learning difficulty. (Source: RCH CPG: Neurofibromatosis type 1)

explanation.summary: Neurofibromatosis type 1 is diagnosed clinically when two or more established criteria are present, among them six or more flat brown macules, skin fold freckling, two or more neurofibromas, optic pathway glioma, Lisch nodules, a characteristic bone lesion and an affected first degree relative. About half of cases arise from new mutations, so an absent family history does not argue against it. Because features accumulate with age, the pigmented macules often appear in infancy while freckling, neurofibromas and Lisch nodules follow through childhood, and a young child may not yet meet criteria. Management is lifelong annual surveillance for treatable complications rather than treatment of the skin.
key_points: Diagnosis is clinical and needs two or more established criteria
Six or more macules over 5 mm plus skin fold freckling meets the threshold
About half of cases are new mutations, so family history is often negative
Annual review covers blood pressure, vision, spine, puberty and development
Routine neuroimaging of an asymptomatic child is not recommended
explanation.pearls: Hypertension in a child with neurofibromatosis type 1 should never be attributed to essential hypertension, because renal artery stenosis and phaeochromocytoma are both over represented and both are correctable once identified.

sources.label: Genetics in Medicine: Revised diagnostic criteria for neurofibromatosis type 1

subtopic_detail: Girl with brief staring episodes reproduced at the bedside by overbreathing and an electroencephalogram showing generalised spike and wave
stem:
You are the general paediatrician reviewing a 7 year old girl whose teacher reports that she blanks out many times a day, stopping mid sentence and staring for a few seconds before carrying straight on as if nothing happened. Her parents say she never falls, never shakes and is never drowsy or confused afterwards.

In clinic you asked her to blow at a paper windmill for three minutes and reproduced an episode lasting eight seconds with eyelid fluttering and no response to her name. Her development, school progress and neurological examination are normal, and an electroencephalogram showed generalised 3 Hz spike and wave discharges with a normal background.

data_table.Examination: Neurological examination unremarkable, no focal deficit, no neurocutaneous stigmata, fundi normal
data_table.Investigations: Electroencephalogram generalised 3 Hz spike and wave on a normal background, no photoparoxysmal response

options.text: Carbamazepine, titrated over two weeks to a usual maintenance dose
options.rationale: Carbamazepine is effective for focal epilepsy but aggravates generalised absence and myoclonic seizures and can precipitate absence status. This is a recognised prescribing trap when brief staring is misread as focal impaired awareness. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Ethosuximide, titrated over two weeks to a usual maintenance dose
options.rationale: For typical childhood absence epilepsy ethosuximide has equivalent seizure freedom to valproate with significantly less attentional impairment, and it is preferred over valproate in girls because of the teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risks of valproate across the reproductive years. It does not cover generalised tonic clonic seizures, so the treatment is revisited if those appear. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Sodium valproate, titrated over two weeks to a usual maintenance dose
options.rationale: Valproate controls absence seizures well and also covers generalised tonic clonic seizures, so it remains an option where those coexist. In a girl it is avoided where an equally effective alternative exists, because of teratogenicity and neurodevelopmental effects that persist as a consideration for decades. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Levetiracetam, titrated over two weeks to a usual maintenance dose
options.rationale: Levetiracetam is widely used in generalised epilepsies and is well tolerated in other respects, but its efficacy specifically against absence seizures is lower than ethosuximide or valproate in comparative trials. It is a later choice rather than a first line agent for this syndrome. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Clobazam, titrated over two weeks to a usual maintenance dose
options.rationale: Clobazam is used as an add on when first line agents fail or during clusters, and tolerance to its effect commonly develops. Starting with it forgoes the agent with the best evidence for attention preserved seizure control in this syndrome. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Childhood absence epilepsy typically begins between four and ten years in a neurologically normal child and produces frequent brief lapses with abrupt onset and offset and no postictal state, which is what separates it from focal impaired awareness seizures. Hyperventilation for two to three minutes provokes an event in most untreated children and is a useful bedside confirmation before the electroencephalogram. The head to head comparative evidence places ethosuximide and valproate ahead of lamotrigine for seizure freedom, with ethosuximide producing less attentional impairment than valproate. Most children remit by adolescence, although a minority develop generalised tonic clonic seizures or evolve to juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, so review of seizure type continues after control is achieved.
key_points: Abrupt onset and offset with no postictal confusion characterises absence
Hyperventilation for two to three minutes provokes an event in most children
The electroencephalogram shows generalised 3 Hz spike and wave
Ethosuximide matches valproate for control with less attentional impairment
Carbamazepine and related sodium channel agents aggravate absence seizures
explanation.pearls: Ethosuximide has no activity against generalised tonic clonic seizures, so the emergence of a convulsion in a child controlled on it is an indication to change agent rather than to increase the dose.

subtopic_detail: Boggy tender scalp swelling with broken hairs and occipital nodes in a child already treated with a topical antifungal cream
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 6 year old boy whose scalp has developed a soft boggy lump over six weeks. His mother has been applying an antifungal cream prescribed a month ago for what was then a scaly patch, and says the hair in that area now comes out when she washes it.

The family has two guinea pigs that arrived shortly before the rash began. He has had no fever and is otherwise well.

data_table.Examination: A 5 cm boggy tender raised plaque on the vertex with overlying pustules and yellow crust, hairs within the plaque broken close to the surface and epilate painlessly, surrounding scale, two tender occipital lymph nodes, no fluctuance on palpation, no cellulitis of the surrounding scalp
data_table.Investigations: Skin scraping and plucked hairs sent for fungal microscopy and culture

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Continue the topical antifungal cream and add a medicated antifungal shampoo
options.rationale: Topical agents cannot penetrate the hair follicle where the organism resides, which is why this lesion has progressed over a month of cream. Antifungal shampoo is a useful adjunct that reduces spore shedding to contacts, but it does not clear the infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Refer for incision and drainage of the swelling under general anaesthesia
options.rationale: Incision and drainage treats a true scalp abscess, which is fluctuant, and this lesion is boggy but not fluctuant because the swelling is a hypersensitivity response rather than a collection of pus. Surgery adds scarring and permanent hair loss to an area that can recover with medical treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Prescribe oral flucloxacillin for ten days and review the scalp at the end of it
options.rationale: Antibacterial treatment addresses the pustules and crust but not the dermatophyte driving them, and the lesion recurs once it is stopped. Bacterial folliculitis of the scalp does not usually produce painless hair epilation or a six week boggy plaque. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Prescribe an oral antifungal agent and treat household contacts and the pets
options.rationale: A boggy plaque with painless hair epilation and occipital nodes is a kerion, the inflammatory form of scalp dermatophyte infection, and it requires a systemic antifungal such as griseofulvin or terbinafine because topicals cannot reach the follicle. Guinea pigs are a common zoophilic source in Australia, so treating the animals and screening household contacts prevents reinfection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Prescribe a potent topical corticosteroid ointment to settle the inflammation
options.rationale: Steroid alone suppresses the inflammatory response while allowing the dermatophyte to spread, producing the altered appearance known as tinea incognito. Short adjunctive oral steroid is occasionally used alongside an antifungal in severe kerion, but never as sole treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

explanation.summary: Scalp dermatophyte infection is the one form of tinea that always requires systemic treatment, because the organism invades the hair shaft and follicle where topical agents cannot reach. It presents along a spectrum from subtle scaling with broken hairs, often mistaken for seborrhoeic dermatitis or alopecia areata, to a kerion, which is a boggy inflammatory mass with pustules and regional lymphadenopathy that is frequently mistaken for a bacterial abscess. Painless epilation of hairs within the lesion is a useful discriminator from bacterial infection. Scrapings and plucked hairs should be sent before starting treatment because the choice and duration of agent differs between Microsporum and Trichophyton species, but treatment is not delayed waiting for culture.
key_points: Scalp tinea always requires a systemic antifungal, never topical alone
Kerion is a hypersensitivity response, not an abscess, and is not drained
Hairs within the lesion epilate painlessly, unlike in bacterial folliculitis
Zoophilic sources include guinea pigs, kittens and puppies
Topical corticosteroid alone produces tinea incognito
explanation.pearls: Griseofulvin remains preferred for Microsporum canis, the species most often acquired from pets, whereas terbinafine clears Trichophyton species in a shorter course, so the culture result determines both agent and duration even though treatment begins empirically.

subtopic_detail: Newborn with a limp arm held internally rotated after a difficult delivery with preserved grasp and an intact clavicle
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a term newborn boy on day one whose right arm lies limp by his side. The birth was complicated by difficulty delivering the shoulders after a prolonged second stage, and his birth weight was 4400 g.

His mother is distressed and asks whether he will ever use the arm and whether an operation is needed now. He is feeding well and is otherwise settled.

data_table.Examination: Right arm held adducted and internally rotated at the shoulder with the elbow extended and the forearm pronated, absent right Moro response with an intact left Moro, grasp reflex present and equal in both hands, no crepitus or tenderness over either clavicle, symmetrical chest expansion with no respiratory distress, pupils equal with no ptosis, right biceps and brachioradialis reflexes absent
data_table.Investigations: Chest and clavicle radiograph shows no fracture and no diaphragmatic elevation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Immobilise the arm across the chest for three weeks and review after that
options.rationale: Prolonged immobilisation was historical practice and causes contracture at the shoulder and elbow, which worsens the long term functional result. Gentle passive movement is started early precisely to prevent that. (Source: RCH CPG: Brachial plexus injury)

options.text: Begin gentle passive movement with physiotherapy and review for biceps recovery
options.rationale: An upper trunk injury affecting the fifth and sixth cervical roots produces this posture with a preserved grasp, and most infants recover spontaneously with physiotherapy to maintain range and prevent contracture. Return of elbow flexion is the accepted marker of a good prognosis, and failure of biceps function to recover by around three months is the trigger for surgical referral. (Source: RCH CPG: Brachial plexus injury)

options.text: Refer immediately for nerve grafting to be performed within the first fortnight
options.rationale: Early exploration is considered only where the whole plexus is involved with a flail insensate arm, or where Horner syndrome or phrenic involvement indicates avulsion. Operating in the first weeks on an injury with a high spontaneous recovery rate exposes the infant to unnecessary surgery. (Source: RCH CPG: Brachial plexus injury)

options.text: Arrange nerve conduction studies in the first week to determine the prognosis
options.rationale: Electrophysiology performed in the first week cannot distinguish neurapraxia from axonal rupture because Wallerian degeneration has not yet occurred, so the result does not guide management. Serial clinical assessment of biceps function is the practical prognostic tool. (Source: RCH CPG: Brachial plexus injury)

options.text: Arrange urgent ultrasound of the shoulder to exclude a proximal humeral injury
options.rationale: Proximal humeral or clavicular injury does cause pseudoparalysis after a difficult delivery and is a reasonable differential, but it produces pain on handling, local swelling or crepitus rather than a fixed posture with absent reflexes. Absent biceps and brachioradialis reflexes with a normal radiograph point to a nerve rather than a bone problem. (Source: RCH CPG: Brachial plexus injury)

explanation.summary: Brachial plexus birth injury complicates roughly one to three per thousand births and is associated with shoulder dystocia, high birth weight and instrumental delivery, although it also occurs after uncomplicated births and after caesarean section. The commonest pattern involves the upper roots and produces the characteristic adducted internally rotated arm with an extended elbow and pronated forearm, while the hand is spared, so grasp remains intact. Features that indicate a more severe or avulsion injury include a flail insensate limb, an ipsilateral Horner syndrome from first thoracic root involvement, and diaphragmatic paralysis from phrenic nerve injury. The majority recover substantially by three months, and recovery of elbow flexion within that window is the accepted prognostic marker used to decide on referral for nerve reconstruction.
key_points: Upper root injury spares the hand, so grasp is preserved
Physiotherapy from the first days prevents contracture during recovery
Return of biceps function by around three months indicates good prognosis
Horner syndrome or diaphragmatic paralysis indicates a severe injury
Immobilisation worsens outcome by causing joint contracture
explanation.pearls: An ipsilateral ptosis and small pupil in a newborn with a weak arm indicates first thoracic root avulsion, which carries a far worse prognosis than an upper trunk injury and warrants early referral to a specialist brachial plexus service rather than watchful waiting.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Brachial plexus birth injury

subtopic_detail: Older boy with a foreskin that was previously retractile and now has a firm pale ring at the tip with spraying and recurrent soreness
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 9 year old boy whose father reports that the end of his foreskin has gone pale and hard over the past year. He used to be able to pull it back for washing and now cannot, his urine comes out as a spray that goes everywhere, and the tip balloons when he goes.

He has had three episodes of a red sore tip in the past twelve months, each treated with a topical preparation. He has no other skin or joint problems.

data_table.Examination: A firm white sclerotic ring at the preputial tip with loss of the normal pliability, the foreskin cannot be retracted at all and the meatus is not visible, no active discharge, the shaft skin and scrotum are unaffected, testes descended bilaterally and of equal volume
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative for leucocytes, nitrites and blood

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure the family and teach gentle daily retraction in the bath at home
options.rationale: Reassurance and gentle hygiene is correct for physiological non retractility, in which the foreskin is soft, pink and simply not yet separated from the glans. A previously retractile foreskin that has become fixed by a firm white ring is an acquired scarring process, not a developmental stage. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreskin care)

options.text: Prescribe a topical corticosteroid ointment to the tight ring twice daily for six weeks
options.rationale: Topical steroid successfully loosens a physiologically tight foreskin in most boys and is the usual first step for that problem. Where the tip is sclerotic and white, steroid alone rarely restores retractility and, more importantly, leaves the underlying scarring process untreated and unconfirmed. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreskin care)

options.text: Refer for circumcision, which is both treatment and gives tissue for diagnosis
options.rationale: A previously retractile foreskin that becomes fixed by a firm white sclerotic ring, with spraying, ballooning and recurrent inflammation, is balanitis xerotica obliterans, the genital form of lichen sclerosus. Circumcision is the definitive treatment and the excised tissue confirms the histological diagnosis, which matters because the meatus and glans need ongoing surveillance. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreskin care)

options.text: Prescribe oral cefalexin for seven days and review the appearance after the course
options.rationale: Oral antibiotics treat an acute bacterial balanitis, which presents with an acutely red, swollen, tender and often discharging prepuce. The current appearance is a chronic sclerotic change with no active infection, and the recurrent sore episodes are a consequence of the underlying process. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange a renal tract ultrasound and review him once the imaging is available
options.rationale: Upper tract imaging would be relevant if there were recurrent urinary infection or a suspicion of obstruction affecting the kidneys, neither of which is present with a negative dipstick and normal growth. Spraying here is caused by a fixed narrow preputial opening rather than by anything upstream. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

explanation.summary: Most tight foreskins in boys are physiological, reflecting incomplete separation of the prepuce from the glans, and they need only reassurance or a course of topical steroid. Balanitis xerotica obliterans is the important exception and is the only absolute medical indication for circumcision in childhood, becoming more likely after about age five. The history that separates them is loss of a foreskin that previously retracted, and the sign is a firm white sclerotic ring replacing the soft preputial tip. Left untreated it can progress to involve the meatus and navicular fossa, producing meatal stenosis and urethral stricture, so boys need follow up after circumcision rather than simple discharge.
key_points: Physiological non retractility improves with age and responds to topical steroid
Loss of previously present retractility suggests an acquired scarring process
A firm white sclerotic preputial ring is the sign of balanitis xerotica obliterans
Circumcision is the definitive treatment and provides histological confirmation
Meatal and urethral involvement can follow, so follow up is required
explanation.pearls: Balanitis xerotica obliterans is the one absolute medical indication for circumcision in boys, and because up to a fifth develop meatal stenosis the urinary stream should be reviewed at follow up rather than assuming the operation has ended the problem.

subtopic_detail: Toddler with outward bowing of the legs and wide wrists whose biochemistry shows a raised parathyroid hormone with low vitamin D
stem:
You are the general paediatrician seeing a 22 month old boy whose legs have bowed outwards over the past six months and who his mother says walks like a sailor. He was breastfed until 18 months without any supplement, and now drinks little milk because of a cows milk protein allergy diagnosed in infancy.

He wears long clothing outdoors and the family spends little time in the sun. There is no family history of bone disease or short stature, and both parents have straight legs.

data_table.Examination: Height on the 10th centile having previously tracked the 40th, symmetrical outward bowing of both tibiae, widened wrists, a palpable ridge at the costochondral junctions, frontal bossing, normal tone and power, no fractures
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.10 mmol/L (2.20 to 2.60), phosphate 0.85 mmol/L (1.20 to 1.80), alkaline phosphatase 980 U/L (100 to 400), parathyroid hormone 16.5 pmol/L (1.6 to 6.9), 25 hydroxyvitamin D 14 nmol/L (greater than 50), creatinine 24 micromol/L (15 to 40), venous bicarbonate 24 mmol/L (22 to 32), wrist radiograph shows cupping and fraying of the distal radial and ulnar metaphyses

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Oral cholecalciferol with calcium supplementation and dietary review
options.rationale: A low 25 hydroxyvitamin D with secondary elevation of parathyroid hormone, low normal calcium and low phosphate is the biochemical signature of nutritional rickets, and the combination of prolonged unsupplemented breastfeeding, dairy avoidance and low sun exposure explains it. Treatment is vitamin D replacement together with calcium, since giving vitamin D alone to a calcium deplete child can precipitate hypocalcaemia as bone mineralisation resumes. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D deficiency)

options.text: Oral phosphate supplements with active vitamin D and endocrine referral
options.rationale: Phosphate with calcitriol treats X linked hypophosphataemic rickets, in which renal phosphate wasting produces a low phosphate with a normal calcium, a normal or only mildly raised parathyroid hormone and a normal 25 hydroxyvitamin D. Here the vitamin D is profoundly low and the parathyroid hormone markedly raised, which is the opposite pattern. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D deficiency)

options.text: Oral sodium bicarbonate with potassium replacement and nephrology referral
options.rationale: Alkali therapy treats the rickets of renal tubular acidosis, which is identified by a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with a low venous bicarbonate. The bicarbonate is 24 mmol/L, which excludes that mechanism. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D deficiency)

options.text: Referral for orthopaedic assessment with a view to guided growth surgery
options.rationale: Surgical correction is considered for persistent pathological bowing after the metabolic cause has been treated, or for a growth plate disorder such as tibia vara. Most bowing from nutritional rickets remodels once mineralisation is restored, so operating first would be premature. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D deficiency)

options.text: Reassurance with repeat measurement of leg alignment in six to twelve months
options.rationale: Watchful waiting suits physiological bowing, which is symmetrical, present from the start of walking, resolves by about age two and has normal biochemistry and radiographs. Metaphyseal cupping and fraying with a raised alkaline phosphatase is pathological and progresses if untreated. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D deficiency)

explanation.summary: Nutritional rickets remains the commonest form of rickets in Australia and is concentrated in breastfed infants without supplementation, children with darker skin, those with limited sun exposure for cultural or medical reasons, and those avoiding dairy. Vitamin D deficiency reduces intestinal calcium absorption, which drives a compensatory rise in parathyroid hormone that maintains calcium at the expense of renal phosphate wasting, producing the characteristic low phosphate with markedly raised alkaline phosphatase. The radiographic hallmarks are metaphyseal cupping, fraying and widening at the fastest growing physes such as the distal radius and knee. The main differential is X linked hypophosphataemic rickets, which shares the low phosphate but has a normal vitamin D and requires entirely different treatment.
key_points: Low 25 hydroxyvitamin D with raised parathyroid hormone indicates nutritional rickets
Low phosphate arises from parathyroid driven renal phosphate wasting
Alkaline phosphatase is markedly raised and is a useful screening test
Calcium is given with vitamin D to prevent hypocalcaemia during remineralisation
Normal vitamin D with low phosphate points to X linked hypophosphataemia instead
explanation.pearls: Starting vitamin D without concurrent calcium in a severely deficient child can precipitate hungry bone hypocalcaemia and seizures within the first days of treatment, which is why replacement is always given as both together.

sources.label: Medical Journal of Australia: Vitamin D and health in adults and children in Australia and New Zealand

subtopic_detail: Child with a severely restricted food range who stops walking and has bleeding swollen gums with bruising around the hair follicles
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 6 year old boy with autism who has stopped walking over the past three weeks and now screams when his legs are moved. His mother says he has eaten only dry biscuits, plain pasta and chicken nuggets for two years, refuses anything with a wet texture, and that his gums bleed when she brushes his teeth.

He has had no fever, no weight loss and no night sweats, and no joint has been swollen or red.

data_table.Examination: Refuses to weight bear, lies with hips and knees flexed, marked tenderness over both distal femora with no joint effusion or warmth, boggy bleeding gum margins around erupted teeth, scattered bruising and corkscrew hairs surrounded by small haemorrhages over both shins, no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly, no pallor of the conjunctivae
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 104 g/L (115 to 135), white cell count 7.2 x10^9/L (5.0 to 15.0), platelets 380 x10^9/L (150 to 450), blood film shows no blasts, C reactive protein 6 mg/L (less than 5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 18 mm/h (less than 20), international normalised ratio 1.0 (0.8 to 1.2), femoral radiographs show generalised osteopenia with dense provisional zones of calcification

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Commence oral ascorbic acid replacement and arrange dietitian involvement
options.rationale: Perifollicular haemorrhage with corkscrew hairs, gingival bleeding and bone pain severe enough to stop a child walking, in a child whose diet has excluded fruit and vegetables for two years, is scurvy. Vitamin C is required for collagen hydroxylation, so deficiency produces fragile vessels and defective osteoid, and symptoms respond within days of replacement. (Source: RCH CPG: Nutrition)

options.text: Commence intravenous flucloxacillin after blood cultures and orthopaedic review
options.rationale: Osteomyelitis is the usual explanation for bone pain with refusal to weight bear, but it is typically unilateral and accompanied by fever and raised inflammatory markers. Afebrile bilateral metaphyseal pain with a C reactive protein of 6 mg/L does not fit, and the gum and skin findings are unexplained by infection. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute osteomyelitis)

options.text: Arrange urgent bone marrow aspiration and refer to paediatric oncology
options.rationale: Leukaemia genuinely presents with bone pain, refusal to walk and bleeding gums, and is the diagnosis that must not be missed. Against it here are a normal white cell count and platelet count, a film without blasts, no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly, and a dietary history that supplies an alternative explanation. (Source: RCH CPG: Nutrition)

options.text: Commence naproxen for suspected juvenile idiopathic arthritis and refer to rheumatology
options.rationale: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis causes joint pain with swelling, warmth and early morning stiffness that eases through the day, and the pain localises to joints rather than to the shafts and metaphyses. There is no effusion or joint warmth, and bleeding gums are not a feature. (Source: RCH CPG: Nutrition)

options.text: Commence cholecalciferol with calcium replacement and repeat the biochemistry
options.rationale: Vitamin D deficiency also causes bone pain and osteopenia in a child with a restricted diet, so it is a reasonable competing nutritional diagnosis and often coexists. It does not produce perifollicular haemorrhage, corkscrew hairs or gingival bleeding, which are specific to defective collagen synthesis. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D deficiency)

explanation.summary: Scurvy is reappearing in Australian paediatric practice in children with severely restricted diets, most often those with autism spectrum disorder, avoidant restrictive food intake disorder or neurodisability. Vitamin C is a cofactor for the hydroxylation of proline and lysine in collagen, so deficiency weakens vessel walls, periosteum and osteoid, producing subperiosteal bleeding that is exquisitely painful and often mistaken for infection, malignancy or non accidental injury. The classic skin findings of perifollicular haemorrhage and corkscrew hairs, along with gingival swelling and bleeding in a child with erupted teeth, are the clue that distinguishes it. Clinical response to replacement is rapid, with pain easing within days and walking usually restored within weeks, and the long term work is on expanding the food range.
key_points: Suspect scurvy in restricted diets lasting more than about three months
Perifollicular haemorrhage and corkscrew hairs are highly suggestive
Subperiosteal bleeding causes bone pain and refusal to weight bear
Normal inflammatory markers and film argue against infection and leukaemia
Symptoms improve within days of vitamin C replacement
explanation.pearls: Gum changes in scurvy only occur around erupted teeth, so an edentulous infant with the same deficiency presents with irritability, pseudoparalysis and leg pain alone and the mouth looks entirely normal.
